explanation: Fires mostly on approximation words right before a number ("about", "roughly", "nearly", "approximately", "on track for roughly"), strongest when a quantity follows. It also fires on unrelated tokens: the initial value in for-loops ("i = 0"), a type cast ("int32"), CJK punctuation, and boilerplate words. Mid and weak activations are scattered and have no clear pattern.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word that is split into several tokens, mostly at the start of proper names (surnames like "Sch"-lichter or "Ro"-que, "Hos"-ni, "Gh"-osn) and of capitalized legal words like "Ind"-ividually. It also fires on the first piece of rare technical words ("n"-aphtha, "radi"-olarians, "ion"-omer). Whole common words fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on a middle subword piece inside foreign proper names, mainly place and person names (Chinese provinces like Sh-"and"-ong, K-"ilk"-enny, Z-"el"-enskiy, B-"ok"-ova, Z-"empl"-ín) and other rare words split into pieces. It also fires weakly on scattered ordinary tokens.

Fires on a word-piece within rare, multi-token proper nouns and technical terms, especially foreign place names, author surnames, and Latin species or medical names (A-"vey"-ron, B-"ör"-nert, Ay-"od"-hya, "sal"-inarium, o-"cul"-ocutaneous). It also fires on some unrelated tokens like "such as", "and Bill", and license or triple strings.

Fires on a head word or word-piece that follows a modifier and forms a compound or set phrase, such as "golf course", "German automobile club", "sports-car", "Football Club", "in fluid", "Unix", or a Russian word piece. It also fires on opening brackets in math and regex code ("Simplify (", "(\\frac", "(["). The pattern is diffuse.

Fires very strongly only inside long runs of repeated characters or digits ("00000000000", "8888", ";;;;;;;;"), on the token that continues or breaks the run. Everything else is below about 10% and is scattered noise.

Fires on tokens inside structured references and boilerplate: the space or number after "Version" in software licenses, "Section" in legal citations, ":" before line numbers in stack traces, and path or namespace separators in code ("/dist", ".Type", "::iterator"). A few unrelated prose tokens also fire.

Fires on the second token of a common fixed multi-word expression or name, where the first word makes it predictable ("See also", "StdAfx.h", "Massachusetts Avenue", "Appeal from", "Royal Astronomical Society", "Ice Age", "ordinary people"). It also fires on the year after a date ("October 1, 1995").

Fires on parameters and template syntax in technical or math text. These include variable symbols in math ("Z", "N", "\\alpha", "sample size"), words in hypothesis or limit phrasing, and C++/Swift generic template brackets and commas ("template<", "<TKey, TValue>"). Fires most on a symbol that names a parameter.

Fires on tokens in Unix and software-packaging boilerplate: NetBSD $-revision headers, "this" in "packaging of this file" or "directory of this source tree" in license text, autoconf macros (AC_), build or platform strings (-mingw32, -p385), Unix paths (/etc, /usr), apt-get, and Homebrew cask syntax.

Fires on the first subword piece of a long word split into several tokens, mostly in scientific or medical terms ("trans"-locations, "Sup"-pressor, "mon"-olayer, "Hy"-ponatremia, "bip"-henyls) and in French or German words and foreign names ("v"-aste, "v"-endredi, "Mitt"-woch). Common whole words fire weakly.

Fires on words that send the reader to more information or a link: "more" in "Learn more", "See more" or "Read More"; "https" or "http" starting a URL after "See" or in a markdown link; "here" in "see here"; and license or header fields like "SPDX-License-Identifier", "$URL$", and "Copyright (".

Fires on assorted tokens in mixed-language text and code: "opensource" in license URLs, sentence-initial connectives in Chinese and French ("而", "Mais"), identifier pieces in Swift, C# and Obj-C code (aDecoder, Product, didFinish), and some medical word-pieces. There is no clear single theme.

Fires on a wide, mixed set of tokens: unit symbols after numbers ("lm W", "per hour"), digits in years and prices, opening quotes or parentheses in code string arguments ("(\"", "('"), function words in academic prose ("whom", "said", "usual"), and acronym pieces. No coherent concept is visible.
